title: Ship-scale collapse of turbulent skin friction

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a durable flow state around a ship that reduces turbulent skin friction—the resistance caused by water rubbing against the hull—to a small fraction of its conventional smooth-hull value. The defining achievement would be a large net propulsion benefit maintained in ordinary service, after accounting for the energy needed to create and sustain that state. The target applies at full ship scale, where Reynolds numbers can be of the order of 10^9.

Concept synthesis: the innovation is defined by its sustained performance, rather than by a particular device or material. A continuous air layer, polymer release, a surface treatment or another method could be a route toward it. The proposed capability must retain its advantage under representative hull roughness, biofouling, seams and waves. Local drag reduction or a short-lived improvement would provide useful progress without demonstrating this complete operational capability.

significance.text: Skin friction can dominate ship resistance. Park et al., published in Scientific Reports on 7 June 2023, describe its contribution as approximately 80% for modern hull forms. This percentage is a share of resistance, not a demonstrated reduction, an established performance requirement or a universal fleet value. It also does not directly specify the share of all onboard fuel consumption attributable to friction. Nevertheless, removing most of a dominant resistance component would offer a strong physical basis for substantially reducing propulsion power at existing service speeds.

The environmental stakes are substantial: the supplied IMO page, citing the Fourth IMO GHG Study 2020, reports that shipping emitted 1,056 million tonnes of CO2 in 2018, approximately 2.89% of global anthropogenic CO2. These figures concern shipping overall and should not be substituted for the smaller voyage-based international-shipping total distinguished by that page. Broad adoption of a durable, net-positive friction-reduction capability could materially reduce propulsion energy and associated emissions, but the resulting fleet-wide savings would depend on vessel suitability, adoption, operating conditions, propulsion efficiency, maintenance and the energy source used.

Evaluative synthesis: calling this a Bessemer-scale advance expresses a judgment about the potential importance of transforming an existing global transport system. It is not a measured economic outcome or a prediction that total shipping costs would fall in proportion to hull resistance. The most direct consequence would be lower propulsion demand at comparable speed and loading; the magnitude of any improvement in freight costs, range or commercial competitiveness would require additional operational and economic evidence.

Friction reduction would not remove wave-making resistance or every other constraint on speed. The scale-effects review associates Froude number with gravity and wave-making, and Reynolds number with viscous effects, while describing interactions between resistance components. Higher speeds might become practical in some circumstances, but neither their magnitude nor the need for a separate breakthrough follows from friction reduction alone. This limits the analogy between removing skin friction and freeing a merchant ship from displacement-hull speed constraints.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is a large, durable reduction of turbulent wall friction at ship Reynolds numbers while preserving a substantial net power benefit throughout representative service. The engineering challenge extends beyond producing a favorable patch of flow: the method must maintain useful performance over enough of the hull, through changing operating conditions, and after its own maintenance and operating demands are counted. Roughness and fouling are material barriers because the scale-effects review documents their substantial influence on resistance. Tolerance of seams, biofouling and a seaway remains part of the proposed target, rather than a demonstrated property of every candidate method.

For polymer-based approaches, the supplied review identifies concrete persistence problems: locally injected polymer can lose its downstream influence, and selected earlier polymer-release coatings lost their drag-reducing effects within days or approximately an hour. These examples show why delivery, replenishment and durability matter. They do not establish that all drag-reduced layers fail at full scale: Park et al. also report sustained service benefits from a replenishing coating. Similarly, the supplied evidence does not establish a universal inability to maintain an air film over a hull. The unresolved challenge is achieving the much stronger combination of magnitude, durability and net operational benefit defined here.

Validation is difficult because conventional reduced-scale ship tests in water cannot simultaneously match full-scale Froude and Reynolds similarity. A model that represents wave-making correctly therefore does not automatically reproduce the ship's viscous-flow conditions. The scale-effects review also discusses numerical approaches, so this limitation should not be generalized into a claim that simultaneous similarity is impossible in every modeling method. Laboratory experiments and computation can support development, but this operational target calls for full-scale evidence with sufficiently reduced uncertainty.

current_state.text: Park et al. (2023) report an estimated equivalent power saving of 11.7% for a frictional-drag-reducing antifouling coating using chemical polymer release, relative to a conventional antifouling coating on a 176,000 DWT bulk carrier. The estimate came from an earlier study analyzing navigation data from November 2014 through December 2019 using ISO 19030 analysis. It is a reported service-data result cited by the 2023 paper, rather than a direct ship-power experiment performed in that paper. The underlying earlier study and service dataset were not supplied for the evidence review, limiting independent assessment of the estimate and its comparison conditions.

The 2023 paper's own laboratory coating specimen achieved a reported skin-friction reduction of 9.49% at 5 m/s. It separately cites an earlier coating result of 13.5%; these two selected results explain the research notes' approximate 9–14% range, but do not establish that range as a comprehensive summary of all experiments. Laboratory skin-friction reduction, total ship resistance reduction and equivalent propulsion-power saving are different quantities and cannot be treated as interchangeable measures of progress.

The laboratory evidence has material measurement limitations. Park et al. describe friction-coefficient uncertainties typically reaching a few tens of percent, associated with acquisition periods limited to several seconds. The supplied review relied on explicit prose and extracted tables; the figures were not visually inspected. These limitations qualify the precision and interpretation of the coating measurements without proving that the reported effect is absent.

Park et al. also describe polymer drag reduction associated with the Toms effect reaching several tens of percent in controlled flows. Their discussion of earlier coatings includes one whose effect almost disappeared after a few days and another whose effect diminished within an hour. These examples establish both the potential of polymer-mediated turbulent-friction reduction and the durability problems encountered by particular implementations. They should be read alongside the reported longer-term vessel result, rather than generalized into a claim that polymer-release coatings cannot function in service.

The supplied research notes attribute additional full-scale air-lubrication results to Hoang, Toda and Sanada's ISOPE 2009 paper: maximum total-resistance reductions of about 11% in ballast and 6% fully loaded on the cement carrier Pacific Seagull in 2008, and approximately 2% net energy saving in an earlier training-ship trial. No retained artifact of that paper was available to the supplied review. Consequently, these figures, dates, loading conditions and metric definitions remain unverified within this record. They are retained as attributed research claims, rather than established measurements from the reviewed evidence; the missing artifact is not evidence that the results are false.

Evidence-bound synthesis: the documented coating results demonstrate useful partial progress, with reported magnitudes substantially below the proposed removal of most skin friction. They do not establish a common 'tenth-scale' distance to completion, because their resistance, friction and power metrics differ. The supplied record contains no bounded freshness-search results, so it cannot establish whether the complete target remained unachieved as of 1 November 2026 or characterize all subsequent developments. MNE-01 is therefore retained as a hypothetical capability target without asserting either its achievement or a verified present-day absence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: one or more in-service merchant ships should sustain a net propulsion-power reduction corresponding to removal of most of the baseline frictional-resistance contribution at their normal service speed, over at least a year of ordinary trading. Before trials begin, the investigators should define numerically what 'most' means, establish the baseline frictional contribution and explain how resistance changes translate into propulsion-power changes. The one-year duration and majority-friction objective are proposed requirements for this concept, not published class rules or thresholds endorsed by the cited papers.
completion_criteria.label: Year-long net propulsion savings equivalent to removing most baseline friction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement protocol: net benefit should account explicitly for the energy used to create, replenish and maintain the flow state. Comparison with a conventional sister ship, or another justified controlled baseline, should address loading, speed, weather, propulsion condition, coating roughness and fouling. Ordinary roughness and fouling should remain represented in the evaluation, while differences between treated and reference vessels must be measured and controlled. Measurement uncertainty, weather normalization and the treatment of maintenance periods should be specified in advance.
completion_criteria.label: Net benefit accounts for flow-state energy against controlled baselines

completion_criteria.text: Full-scale operational validation and explicit uncertainty assessment have a technical basis in the scale-effects review, which emphasizes reducing uncertainties sufficiently to demonstrate energy-saving devices under validated full-scale operating conditions. A convincing evaluation should connect measured propulsion savings with evidence that reduced hull friction is responsible, accounting for interactions with the propulsion system and other resistance components.
completion_criteria.label: Full-scale propulsion savings attributable to reduced hull friction with uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: repeat the result across independent trial periods and, where feasible, additional vessels or installations, using methods and sufficient data that others can scrutinize. Report the demonstrated envelope of speeds, loading, sea states, roughness and fouling, together with deterioration, recovery and maintenance requirements. A flat-plate experiment or a short calm-water trial showing only a few percent saving would not establish the stated magnitude and durability. Partial air coverage should not itself disqualify a method if it achieves the required net performance. Finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within that envelope, not universal performance on every hull or in every ocean condition.
completion_criteria.label: Independent trials reproduce savings and report the demonstrated operational envelope

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MNE-02, 'Merchant ships freed from the displacement-hull speed barrier,' overlaps with MNE-01 through the overall resistance and power budget. MNE-01 targets turbulent skin friction; MNE-02's title concerns the broader constraints on displacement-hull speed. Reducing friction could help enable higher speed, but does not demonstrate removal of wave-making constraints. The supplied review supports that physical distinction, while the absence of a full MNE-02 record prevents a more exact comparison of proposed mechanisms or completion criteria.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-03, 'Seawater magnetohydrodynamic propulsion at propeller-class efficiency,' concerns propulsion efficiency and thrust generation, whereas MNE-01 concerns the hull resistance that propulsion must overcome. They could be complementary, but demonstrating either would not establish the other. MNE-04, 'Controlled, sustained supercavitating travel,' shares an interest in altering the surrounding flow to reduce resistance; its title describes a controlled cavity-travel regime, which should not be equated with every air-lubrication layer or polymer-mediated friction reduction.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-05, 'Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing,' MNE-06, 'Through-seawater links beyond the acoustic range–rate ceiling,' and MNE-10, 'Coherent observability of the deep-ocean volume,' concern positioning, communication and observation rather than hull friction. They might support monitoring or operation of marine systems benefiting from lower drag, but none of their titles makes them a prerequisite for MNE-01 or an alternative demonstration of its capability.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-07, 'Persistent abyssal work, with depth no longer the cost driver,' and MNE-08, 'Work-class underwater vehicles powered by the ocean,' concern underwater operating endurance, work and energy supply. Lower drag could help some mobile systems, but a merchant-ship result would not establish their depth tolerance or energy autonomy. MNE-09, 'Storm-stable floating land in the open ocean,' shares an exposure to severe marine conditions, while addressing stability and habitability rather than propulsion resistance. These comparisons are limited to the supplied titles.

Identity clarification: the research associates an unspecified historical item 1 with MNE-01. That item was not supplied, so its exact overlap cannot be verified. The present record preserves MNE-01's identity and treats air layers, polymers and surface treatments as possible means toward its flow-state target without merging or deleting any roster entry.

brief.title: Ships that lose most of their hull friction
possible: Ships could carry cargo at their usual speeds using much less propulsion power. Water rubbing against the hull would cause only a small fraction of its usual resistance, and the savings would remain large after powering and maintaining the system.
The benefit would last through ordinary service, including waves, hull seams, rough surfaces and organisms growing on the hull. Air layers, coatings or other methods could provide it.
why: Hull friction can account for most of a ship’s resistance. Removing most of it would substantially reduce the power needed to keep moving, giving ship operators a way to cut propulsion energy use.
Widespread use could reduce shipping’s associated emissions. The change would affect an existing global transport system that moves goods by sea.

milestones.label: Year-long savings equivalent to removing most hull friction
milestones.explanation: Ships in ordinary trade would have to sustain net propulsion savings equivalent to removing most baseline hull friction for a year. This would establish the required magnitude and durability.

milestones.label: Net savings against a controlled comparison
milestones.explanation: A controlled comparison would have to count energy spent creating and maintaining the flow while accounting for operating conditions and hull condition. This would establish how much power the method actually saves.

milestones.label: Full-scale savings traced to reduced hull friction
milestones.explanation: Full-scale measurements would have to link propulsion savings to reduced hull friction, with stated uncertainty and allowance for other resistance and propulsion effects. This would establish what caused the benefit.

milestones.label: Independent trials reproduce savings across stated operating conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent trials would have to reproduce savings and report the conditions tested, deterioration, recovery and maintenance needs. This would establish how broadly the demonstrated benefit holds.

uncertain: The fraction of friction that counts as “most,” acceptable measurement uncertainty and required operating conditions remain undefined.
The relationship between the laboratory friction reductions and their substantial measurement uncertainty needs closer assessment.
Whether any method can sustain the required combination of friction reduction, durability and net savings across ordinary service remains open.

page.title: Ship-scale turbulent skin-friction reduction
page.definition: A full-size ship sustains removal of more than half its hull-integrated turbulent skin friction while consuming less total propulsion-system energy in service. Skin friction is resistance caused by water shearing against the hull; hull-integrated means summed over the hull surface.

goal.need: IMO estimates that shipping emitted 1,056 million tonnes of CO2 in 2018, 2.89% of global anthropogenic CO2; voyage-based international shipping accounted for 740 million tonnes. Hoang and colleagues describe friction as nearly 70% of total resistance for low-speed ships. Reducing this component addresses a major propulsion load, although friction reduction, total-resistance reduction and net fuel savings are different quantities.

figures.note: International shipping is included within all shipping; the rows must not be added.

statements.quote: The goal is the development of radical skin friction drag reduction sustained over time periods that are operationally relevant.

completion.title: A ship removes more than half its hull skin friction while using less total propulsion energy in service.
completion.criterion: On a full-size ship, hull-integrated skin-friction resistance is more than 50% below the corresponding smooth, fully wetted baseline at matched speed, loading and hull geometry. Total energy for propulsion and drag reduction, including injection and replenishment, is lower than baseline. Both inequalities remain satisfied after measurement uncertainty is included throughout a prospectively specified service interval and operating envelope representing waves, seams, roughness and fouling. The sources supply no universal minimum duration or service envelope.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; no external body located defines this combined completion test.
completion.basis: Searched DARPA FDR and DRAG goals, IMO efficiency guidance, ISO 19030, ITTC trial guidance and Navy readiness criteria; no cross-technology numerical completion test was found. More than 50% is the narrowest numerical interpretation of removing most friction, explicitly an Atlas threshold. The magnitude, net-energy and service requirements must be demonstrated together; neither a local friction measurement nor a ship-power saving alone establishes them.

milestones.title: A hull-friction-reduction mechanism passes laboratory proof of concept, corresponding to TRL 3.
milestones.criterion: Laboratory experiments validate the critical physical function of a drag-reducing element: technology readiness level (TRL) 3. Park and colleagues, published on 7 June 2023, reported 9.49% skin-friction reduction for their polymer-releasing coating specimen at 5 m/s. This result bears on laboratory feasibility; the authors did not assign it a TRL.
milestones.set_by: DoD generic readiness scale, GAO-05-255 Table 9; threshold tabulated.

milestones.title: A hull-friction-reduction prototype demonstrates its function in a relevant environment, reaching TRL 6.
milestones.criterion: A representative system or subsystem prototype demonstrates its function under relevant conditions: TRL 6. Experiments published on 10 October 2008 provide large-scale evidence: Elbing and colleagues measured air-layer friction reduction exceeding 80% over their smooth flat-plate model at speeds up to 15.3 m/s. Stable air layers also formed on the fully roughened model up to 12.5 m/s, requiring approximately 50% more volumetric airflow. These are model results, without an assigned TRL or demonstrated whole-ship net saving.
milestones.set_by: DoD generic readiness scale, GAO-05-255 Table 9; threshold tabulated.

milestones.title: An integrated ship-friction-reduction prototype operates aboard a ship in its operational environment, at TRL 7.
milestones.criterion: An integrated system prototype demonstrates its function in an operational environment: TRL 7. Hoang and colleagues reported measurements on one cement carrier, Pacific Seagull, from 6 January 2008 to 11 January 2008. Maximum inferred total-resistance reductions were approximately 11% in ballast and 6% fully loaded, assuming unchanged thrust deduction with air injection. The result bears on shipboard demonstration; it is neither a formal TRL assignment nor a measurement of hull-integrated friction removal.
milestones.set_by: DoD generic readiness scale, GAO-05-255 Table 9; threshold tabulated.

milestones.title: The finished ship-friction-reduction installation passes qualification against its design specification, at TRL 8.
milestones.criterion: The completed installation demonstrates conformity with its design specification in its final configuration and expected conditions: TRL 8. This is the qualification stage before successful operational use of the finished system. The generic readiness definition supplies no friction-reduction percentage, qualification duration or required sea state.
milestones.set_by: DoD generic readiness scale, GAO-05-255 Table 9; threshold tabulated.

not_found: No external completion test was found combining a hull-integrated friction-reduction percentage, net energy savings and a specified service duration and envelope.
No drag-specific qualification ladder was found; the milestones use published generic readiness stages without assigning formal readiness levels to the cited experiments.

The DARPA DRAG solicitation attachments were unavailable through the opened SAM.gov page.

results.finding: One polymer-releasing coating specimen achieved 9.49% skin-friction reduction.
results.detail: The water-tunnel experiment measured reduction at 5 m/s and corroborated PEG release. The authors did not assign a TRL; coated-specimen friction measurements had relatively large uncertainty.
results.quote: In the concurrent measurement of skin friction, the present FDR-SPC specimen exhibited a skin friction reduction ratio of 9.49%.

results.finding: One 36 m model ship, tested three times per condition, achieved 28% friction reduction over its air-lubricated bottom.
results.detail: The model was towed at 8.0 m/s in a test tank using bubble injection. This demonstrates friction reduction under relevant flow conditions, but the paper does not establish that the setup is a representative TRL 6 prototype or assign it a TRL.

results.finding: One module carrier tested an air-lubrication prototype at sea, achieving a maximum reported net energy saving of 12%.
results.detail: The prototype operated during shipboard sea trials. Net savings accounted for blower electricity; the source does not assign a formal TRL or measure hull-integrated friction removal.

results.finding: One chemical tanker with Silverstream air lubrication achieved an estimated 4.5% net power saving in service.
results.detail: The estimate is for laden operation at 14 knots, using filtered monitoring data and corrections for compressor power and estimated unit drag. The paper does not formally assign TRL 7 or measure hull-integrated friction removal. Independent verification is reported for separate sea trials, not the long-term estimate.

results.finding: One Diamond Princess air-lubrication retrofit achieved over 5% net efficiency improvement in final contract trials.
results.detail: Trials at design service speed exceeded original performance expectations and were verified by Lloyd’s Register. The source does not establish conformity with the installation’s full design specification or qualification under expected conditions.
